title: Home inspector radon reduction and radon-resistant features practice questions
description: Practice questions on EPA radon reduction guidance: contractors, contracts, reduction methods, checking the work, new homes and radon in water.

questions.question: In a state without regulations covering radon mitigation, what does EPA recommend a radon mitigation system conform to?

options.A: The radon fan manufacturer's installation leaflet
options.B: EPA's most current voluntary consensus-based standards
options.C: The home inspector's written report
options.D: The buyer's mortgage lender's requirements

questions.explanation: The Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide says: "In states without regulations covering mitigation, EPA recommends that the system conform to EPA's most current voluntary consensus-based standards."

source.title: EPA: Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-24/001, revised March 2024)

questions.question: A homeowner plans to have the same firm do the radon testing and install the mitigation system. What does the Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide say about this?

options.A: EPA forbids one firm from doing both jobs
options.B: There is no concern if the firm is certified in the state
options.C: The buyer must pay for the testing separately
options.D: A potential conflict of interest exists, and some states may require the homeowner to sign a waiver

questions.explanation: The guide says "a potential conflict of interest exists if the same person or firm performs the testing and installs the mitigation system. Some states may require the homeowner to sign a waiver in such cases."

source.title: EPA: Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-24/001, revised March 2024)

questions.question: What does EPA recommend the mitigation contractor do before beginning any radon-reduction work?

options.A: Review the radon measurement results
options.B: Install a second vent fan as a backup
options.C: Obtain written approval from EPA
options.D: Replace the home's combustion appliances

questions.explanation: "EPA recommends that the mitigation contractor review the radon measurement results before beginning any radon-reduction work."

source.title: EPA: Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-24/001, revised March 2024)

questions.question: Before any radon reduction work starts, what does the Consumer's Guide say you should make sure of in the contract?

options.A: That it is signed by the home's next buyer
options.B: That it waives the contractor's liability insurance
options.C: That everything in it matches the original proposal
options.D: That it is filed with the state radon office

questions.explanation: The guide says: "Ask the contractor to prepare a contract before any work starts. Read the contract before you sign it. Make sure everything in the contract matches the original proposal."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: Which kind of radon reduction method does EPA generally recommend?

options.A: Methods that prevent the entry of radon
options.B: Methods that reduce radon only after it has entered the home
options.C: Sealing cracks as the only step
options.D: Opening lower-floor windows as a permanent fix

questions.explanation: The Consumer's Guide says: "EPA generally recommends methods that prevent the entry of radon."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A homeowner may later sell the house. Which item does the Consumer's Guide list as important information that should appear in the radon reduction contract?

options.A: A promise that the buyer will keep the fan running
options.B: The name of the buyer's real estate agent
options.C: A declaration stating whether any warranties or guarantees are transferable if you sell your home
options.D: A copy of the seller's lead-based paint disclosure

questions.explanation: Among the important contract information the guide lists "A declaration stating whether any warranties or guarantees are transferable if you sell your home."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: According to the Consumer's Guide, what do the diagnostic tests a contractor may charge for help determine?

options.A: The home's market value
options.B: What type of radon reduction system should be used
options.C: Whether the seller must disclose radon to buyers
options.D: Whether the home qualifies for a tax credit

questions.explanation: The guide says contractors "may charge for diagnostic tests. These tests help determine what type of radon reduction system should be used".

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A contractor bidding on active subslab suction for a basement home says several suction pipes are always required. What does the Consumer's Guide say decides the number and location of suction pipes?

options.A: One pipe is always needed for each room above the slab
options.B: Four pipes are always needed, one at each corner of the slab
options.C: Only the size of the lot the home sits on
options.D: How easily air can move in the crushed rock or soil under the slab and the strength of the radon source; often, only a single suction point is needed

questions.explanation: The guide says "The number and location of suction pipes that are needed depends on how easily air can move in the crushed rock or soil under the slab and on the strength of the radon source. Often, only a single suction point is needed."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: What does passive subslab suction rely on, instead of a fan, to draw radon up from below the home?

options.A: A heat recovery ventilator
options.B: A sump pump
options.C: Open basement windows
options.D: Natural pressure differentials and air currents

questions.explanation: The guide says passive subslab suction "relies on natural pressure differentials and air currents instead of a fan to draw radon up from below the home."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A homeowner caulked every visible crack in the basement floor years ago and asks why EPA does not count sealing alone as a radon fix. Which reason does the Consumer's Guide give?

options.A: It is difficult to identify and permanently seal the places where radon is entering, and normal settling of the home opens new entry routes and reopens old ones
options.B: Sealing increases the loss of conditioned air from the home
options.C: Sealing makes other radon reduction techniques less effective
options.D: Sealing can be used only in homes with crawlspaces

questions.explanation: The Consumer's Guide says EPA does not "recommend the use of sealing alone to reduce radon because, by itself, sealing has not been shown to lower radon levels significantly or consistently. It is difficult to identify and permanently seal the places where radon is entering. Normal settling of your home opens new entry routes and reopens old ones."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A contractor proposes to reduce radon in a crawlspace home by drawing air directly from the crawlspace with a fan, without covering the earth floor. What does the Consumer's Guide say about this technique?

options.A: It is the most effective way to reduce radon levels in crawlspace homes
options.B: It generally does not work as well as submembrane suction and requires special attention to combustion appliance backdrafting and sealing the crawlspace from other portions of the home
options.C: It lowers energy costs because it keeps conditioned air in the home
options.D: It works without a fan, using only natural air currents

questions.explanation: The guide calls it "Another less-favorable option is active crawlspace depressurization, which involves drawing air directly from the crawlspace using a fan" and says "This technique generally does not work as well as submembrane suction and requires special attention to combustion appliance backdrafting and sealing the crawlspace from other portions of the home." It also "may result in increased energy costs due to loss of conditioned air from the home."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: When does the Consumer's Guide say house or room pressurization should be considered?

options.A: As the first choice in every home
options.B: Only in crawlspace homes
options.C: Only after the other, more-common techniques have not sufficiently reduced radon
options.D: Only while the home is listed for sale

questions.explanation: Because it brings in more outdoor air, "this technique should only be considered after the other, more-common techniques have not sufficiently reduced radon."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: The Consumer's Guide says a radon system's exhaust fan must not be located in or below a livable area. Where does it say, for instance, the fan should be installed?

options.A: In a finished basement used as living space
options.B: In the main living area of the home
options.C: In a bedroom closet
options.D: In unconditioned space

questions.explanation: The guide says "The exhaust fan must not be located in or below a livable area. For instance, it should be installed in unconditioned space."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A contractor turns on the fan of a new active radon reduction system at noon, and the homeowner wants to start the post-mitigation test an hour later. What does the Consumer's Guide say about when that test should be done?

options.A: Within 30 days of system installation, but no sooner than 24 hours after the system is in operation with the fan on
options.B: As soon as the fan is on, since the system works right away
options.C: Only after the system has run for a full heating season
options.D: Only if the contractor's own test shows a high level

questions.explanation: The guide says "A post-mitigation radon test should be done within 30 days of system installation, but no sooner than 24 hours after your system is in operation with the fan on, if it has one."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: The contractor may do a post-mitigation test, but the guide recommends an independent follow-up measurement too. What does it say an independent tester, or measuring yourself, will do?

options.A: Make the system's warranty transferable
options.B: Eliminate any potential conflict of interest
options.C: Replace the need for a warning device
options.D: Satisfy EPA's licensing requirement

questions.explanation: The guide says "Having an independent tester perform the test, or conducting the measurement yourself, will eliminate any potential conflict of interest."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.topic: Living with a radon reduction system
questions.question: A homeowner with an active radon reduction system wants to save electricity. What does the Consumer's Guide say about the fan?

options.A: It may be switched off during summer months
options.B: It should be run only at night
options.C: It should NEVER be turned off; it must run continuously for the system to work correctly
options.D: It may be turned off once a test shows a low level

questions.explanation: The guide says: "Remember, the fan should NEVER be turned off; it must run continuously for the system to work correctly."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.topic: Living with a radon reduction system
questions.question: What does the Consumer's Guide say a seller should do when the home has a radon reduction system?

options.A: Inform potential buyers and supply them with information about the system's operation and maintenance
options.B: Remove the system before closing
options.C: Turn the fan off during the buyer's inspection
options.D: Have the system certified by EPA

questions.explanation: The guide says: "If you are selling a home that has a radon reduction system, inform potential buyers and supply them with information about your system's operation and maintenance."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)

questions.question: A new home built with passive radon-resistant features tests at 4 pCi/L or more after occupancy. What does the Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide say can be done?

options.A: The gravel layer must be replaced
options.B: A vent fan can easily be added to the passive system to make it an active system
options.C: The plastic sheeting must be removed
options.D: Nothing, because passive systems cannot be upgraded

questions.explanation: The guide says "If you have a test result of 4 pCi/L or more, a vent fan can easily be added to the passive system to make it an active system and further reduce radon levels."

source.title: EPA: Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-24/001, revised March 2024)

questions.question: In which homes does the Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide say the gas-permeable layer of a radon-resistant home is used?

options.A: Only in homes with crawlspace foundations
options.B: Only in homes over three stories
options.C: Only in homes with private wells
options.D: Only in homes with basement and slab-on-grade foundations

questions.explanation: The guide says "This gas-permeable layer is used only in homes with basement and slab-on-grade foundations; it is not used in homes with crawlspace foundations."

source.title: EPA: Home Buyer's and Seller's Guide to Radon (EPA 402/K-24/001, revised March 2024)

questions.question: What does the Consumer's Guide say about point-of-use radon treatment devices?

options.A: They treat all water entering the home's distribution system
options.B: They are effective in reducing the risk from breathing radon released into the air from all water used in the home
options.C: They only treat a small portion of the water you use and are not effective in reducing the risk from breathing radon released into the air from all water used in the home
options.D: They are the only treatment EPA recognizes for private wells

questions.explanation: The guide says point-of-use devices "only treat a small portion of the water you use" and "are not effective in reducing the risk from breathing radon released into the air from all water used in the home."

source.title: EPA: Consumer's Guide to Radon Reduction (EPA 402/K-10/005, 2025 edition)
